title: Short Essays
description: Ten calm reflective essays on everyday subjects: walking slowly, letters and messages, old things, being bored, mistakes, the kitchen table, home, disagreement, small errands and children's questions.

lessons.title: In Praise of Walking Slowly
lessons.summary: After hurting an ankle, the writer learns that a slow walk lets us see and absorb the world around us.
lessons.text:
Most of us walk the way we eat lunch at our desks: quickly, without noticing, and with our minds somewhere else. The walk is only the time between two places, and the sooner it is over, the better. I would probably still walk that way if I had not hurt my ankle one winter.

For six weeks, my ankle was too sore for anything but a slow walk around the neighborhood. The doctor said it would heal in time; in the meantime, slow was the only speed I had. At first, I hated it. My ankle was sore, my patience was short, and the streets seemed to stretch on forever.

Then, somewhere in the third week, something changed. What I began to notice was not the distance but the details. A man was cutting his lawn in perfectly straight lines. At the edge of town, where the houses end and the fields begin, stands an old red barn that I had driven past for years without really seeing it. Walking slowly, I saw that someone had painted a white horse above the barn door, and that birds flew in and out under its roof all day.

There is, of course, a fair argument against walking slowly. Most of us have jobs, children and long lists of things to do. If you have twenty minutes to get to work, you cannot spend forty admiring other people's lawns.

Still, a slow walk does something that a fast one cannot. When we hurry, we see only what is useful: the traffic light, the corner, the time on our phone. When we slow down, we begin to absorb the world around us instead of simply moving through it. We absorb the smell of cut grass and the color of the light late in the afternoon. We learn to distinguish one bird's song from another's, and to distinguish the pale green of early spring from the deeper green of June.

Walking slowly also changed the map of my town. The field behind the barn had always seemed like the frontier of my small world. On foot, the frontier moved. Past the field I found a narrow road, a stream and what English poets used to call a dale, a wide and gentle valley, with sheep in it. I had lived ten minutes from that dale for eight years.

In the meantime, my ankle healed, and on most working days I walk fast again. But on weekends, I still take one slow walk, and not once have I regretted it. Nothing magnificent happens on these walks. And yet the ordinary things I pass, seen slowly, are magnificent in their own quiet way.

What, then, is the essence of walking slowly? The essence of it, I think, is attention: the simple decision to be where you are, while you are there.

Questions:
Why did the writer start walking slowly?
He hurt his ankle, and it was too sore for a fast walk.
What did the writer notice about the old barn?
He noticed a white horse painted above the door and birds flying under its roof.
What does a slow walk allow us to do, according to the writer?
It allows us to absorb the world around us and to distinguish small details.
What did the writer find beyond the field?
He found a narrow road, a stream and a dale with sheep in it.
What does the writer think is the essence of walking slowly?
He thinks it is attention: the decision to be where you are, while you are there.

lessons.title: Letters and Messages
lessons.summary: The writer weighs fast, useful messages against slow, personal letters and decides that each has its place.
lessons.text:
Let me begin with a confession: I have not written a real letter, on paper, in more than ten years. I send dozens of messages every day, and so, I suspect, do you. Some people say that messages have killed the letter. Frankly, I do not believe that, but I do believe that something has been lost.

First, let us be fair to the message. Messages are fast, cheap and easy. When my sister had her first baby, I saw a photo of my new nephew before he was an hour old, and our cousins abroad likewise saw him within minutes. A hundred and fifty years ago, the fastest way to send such news was the telegraph, and because every word of a telegraph cost money, people kept it short: BABY BOY BORN. ALL WELL. A modern message is, in a sense, the telegraph made free. It is also far more sophisticated: a single sophisticated message can carry a voice, a photo and a map in a few seconds.

Rarely, though, does a message carry the person who sent it. A letter is a physical object, shaped by one particular hand. My grandmother, who hated to waste paper, wrote across the full width of every page, and you could recognize her letters by that width alone. She closed each one with red wax, pressing a small metal stamp into the warm wax to leave the shape of a rose. It is precisely this effort that makes a letter feel authentic. It tells the reader: you were worth my time.

Letters are also more honest emotionally. When we write by hand, we cannot delete, so we tend to think first and to say what we really mean. Many people who would never type "I miss you" can write it easily on paper. Emotionally, a letter is a slower and deeper conversation. The writer chooses each word with care, and the reader, likewise, reads each word with care.

Letters also last. My grandmother's letters are still in a box in my closet. My messages from three years ago are lost somewhere inside an old phone, and frankly, I could not find them if I tried.

Must we, then, choose between the two? I do not think so. The message is wonderful for news, plans and jokes. The letter, the more authentic form, is better for what matters most: thanks, apologies, love and goodbyes.

So here is a second, happier confession. Last week, I bought a box of good writing paper. Someday, when my nephew is old enough to read, I want him to find a letter addressed to him, in my own hand. And someday, perhaps, he will keep it in a box of his own.

Questions:
What is the writer's first confession?
He has not written a real letter on paper in more than ten years.
Why did people keep telegraph messages short?
They kept them short because every word of a telegraph cost money.
How did the writer's grandmother close her letters?
She closed them with red wax and pressed a small metal stamp into it to leave the shape of a rose.
Why are letters more honest emotionally?
We cannot delete when we write by hand, so we think first and say what we really mean.
What does the writer want to do someday?
He wants to write a letter to his nephew, in his own hand.

lessons.title: Why We Keep Old Things
lessons.summary: A garage full of old things leads the writer to a simple rule for what to keep and what to let go.
lessons.text:
Every family has a drawer, a closet or a garage full of things that nobody uses. In my parents' house, it is the garage. There, on metal shelves, sit a broken radio, three lamps without shades, my mother's wedding dress in a satin bag and a canvas tent that has not been used since 1994. My father calls it all junk. My mother calls it "our history." Both of them, I think, are partly right.

The case for throwing things away deserves to be heard first. Old things take up space, and sooner or later they become a job for somebody else. When a friend's grandmother died, her children were her heirs, but what the heirs received was mostly work: boxes of magazines, jars of buttons and forty years of birthday cards. There is a stark difference between a few treasured objects and a room full of junk, and it is usually the heirs who have to decide where that line lies. Another friend of mine boasts that everything she owns fits into a small car. I used to think this was a strange thing to boast about. Now I understand it: she can move in an afternoon.

And yet, when I open the satin bag in my parents' garage, I am not looking at junk. I am looking at the summer day, years before I was born, when my parents were married. On the canvas of the tent, my father wrote the name of every lake where we camped, and reading that list is like reading the story of my childhood. In the kitchen, there is also a heavy glass from which my grandfather drank a small whiskey every Christmas. Nobody in the family drinks whiskey anymore, but nobody would dream of giving the glass away.

What we keep, in other words, is rarely the object itself. It is the memory attached to it. A small child will clutch an old blanket long after it has stopped being warm, because the blanket means safety. Adults are not so different; we simply clutch our treasures less openly.

So which is wiser, to keep or to let go? The stark truth is that we cannot keep everything, and we should not ask our heirs to carry what we could not sort ourselves. But neither should we throw away the few things that hold our stories. My own rule is simple: I keep the objects that would make me tell a story if a visitor picked them up. The remainder can go.

Last summer, my parents tried this rule. They kept the dress, the tent and the glass, and gave the remainder away. My father says the garage has never looked better. My mother says it still holds our history. This time, they are both completely right.

Questions:
What does the writer's father call the things in the garage, and what does his mother call them?
His father calls them junk, and his mother calls them "our history."
What did the heirs of the friend's grandmother receive?
They received mostly work: magazines, buttons and forty years of birthday cards.
What did the writer's father write on the canvas of the tent?
He wrote the name of every lake where the family camped.
Why does a small child clutch an old blanket?
A child clutches it because the blanket means safety.
What is the writer's rule for keeping things?
He keeps the objects that would make him tell a story, and he lets the remainder go.

lessons.title: The Value of Being Bored
lessons.summary: The writer admits that being bored is unpleasant but argues that a little empty time feeds the mind.
lessons.text:
When did you last feel truly bored? I do not mean busy or tired, but bored: with nothing to do, nothing to read and nothing on a screen. Many of us cannot remember. We carry a cure for being bored in our pockets, and we use it at the first sign of trouble. Watch people waiting by an office microwave. One minute is not a long time, yet hardly anyone can stand by the microwave without taking out a phone.

As a child, I was bored often. On Sunday afternoons at my grandmother's house, nothing happened between 2 o'clock and 5 o'clock except the slow ticking of a clock in the hall. The frustration of those hours was real. But somewhere around 4 o'clock, the frustration usually gave way to something else. I built houses out of playing cards, invented games and once drew the map of a country that existed only in my head.

To be fair, being bored is not pleasant, and it is not always useful. For a lonely older person, long empty days are a burden, not a gift, and many bored hours are simply wasted.

Even so, a little of it seems to do us good. In several studies, researchers asked people to do something dull, such as copying numbers from a list for fifteen minutes. Afterward, these people often came up with more creative ideas than people who had skipped the task. It seems that the feeling induced by a dull task sends the mind looking for something better, so that a mood induced by having nothing to do becomes a kind of fuel. Many people know this from experience: a mathematical problem that resists them at a desk suddenly solves itself while they are washing the dishes. A mathematical mind, like any other, needs empty moments to connect its ideas.

The trouble is that we have learned to suppress the feeling before it can do its work. We suppress it so quickly that we never find out what the mind would have done with the empty time.

I do not suggest that we throw our phones into a river. My suggestion is smaller. Just as we allot time to work and sleep, we might allot a little time each week to doing nothing: a walk without music, a train ride without a screen, a minute by the microwave with only our thoughts. The time we have allotted will not always be inspiring. But the most inspiring ideas I have had in recent years came when I had nothing better to do. If I had not been bored so often as a child, I doubt I would be a writer today.

Questions:
What do many people do while they wait by the microwave?
They take out a phone, even though they only have to wait a minute.
What did the writer do on Sunday afternoons after the frustration passed?
He built houses out of playing cards, invented games and once drew the map of a country that existed only in his head.
What happened in the studies after people did a dull task?
They often came up with more creative ideas than people who had skipped the task.
Why do we never find out what the mind would do with empty time?
We suppress the feeling of being bored too quickly.
What does the writer suggest that we do?
He suggests that we allot a little time each week to doing nothing.

lessons.title: Learning from Mistakes
lessons.summary: The writer compares blaming people for mistakes with studying them openly, and argues for treating mistakes as information.
lessons.text:
All of us make mistakes, and most of us are told from childhood that we should learn from them. The advice is good, but it is easier to give than to follow. When something goes wrong, our first instinct is rarely to learn. It is to hide the mistake or to find someone else to blame.

Consider what often happens at work when a project fails. Within an hour, someone has made an accusation, and each accusation produces a defense. Soon everyone is protecting themselves instead of understanding what went wrong. In the worst cases, somebody is asked for a resignation, as though a resignation could repair the problem. The person who resigned leaves, and the flaw that caused the failure stays exactly where it was.

There is a real argument for this approach. People need to be responsible for what they do, and a repeat offender, who keeps making the same error, cannot simply be forgiven every time. I should admit that I am a repeat offender myself: for years, I left my keys in the front door at least once a month.

And yet some fields that cannot afford mistakes have chosen a different path. In many hospitals, surgical teams meet regularly to discuss operations that went wrong, or nearly did. The aim is not to punish anyone but to find the flaw in the system: a confusing label, a tired team, a step that was easy to skip. The effectiveness of these meetings depends on honesty, and honesty depends on safety. If doctors expected punishment, they would hide their errors; because they expect to be heard, they speak. That effectiveness is one reason why surgical care has become so much safer.

In private life, too, it helps to distinguish a mistake made in ignorance from one made without care. Ignorance is not a crime; it is simply the state of not yet knowing. A child who touches a hot pan learns more in a second than from a hundred warnings, and nobody blames her for her ignorance.

What matters most is how we rebound. Children rebound from failure quickly: they fall off a bike, cry for a minute and climb back on. Adults take longer. Some of us even become resigned to our weaknesses, deciding that we are simply "bad with money" or "bad at languages."

I would like a healthier view to prevail: that a mistake is information, not a judgment. Only when we stop treating errors as something to hide can we start treating them as lessons. If that view were to prevail in our homes and offices, we would still make mistakes. But we would rarely make the same one twice.

Questions:
What is our first instinct when something goes wrong, according to the writer?
Our first instinct is to hide the mistake or to find someone else to blame.
What happens to the flaw when someone is asked for a resignation?
The flaw that caused the failure stays exactly where it was.
Why does the writer call himself a repeat offender?
For years, he left his keys in the front door at least once a month.
What does the effectiveness of the surgical teams' meetings depend on?
It depends on honesty, and honesty depends on safety.
What view does the writer hope will prevail?
He hopes that people will see a mistake as information, not as a judgment.

lessons.title: The Kitchen Table
lessons.summary: The writer argues that the plain kitchen table, not the living room, is the true center of a home.
lessons.text:
Ask people where the center of their home is, and many will name the living room, with its couch and its television. I would argue for a plainer place: the kitchen table. Ours is made of pine, one leg is slightly short, and its surface carries the marks of thirty years of homework, birthday candles and spilled tea. Yet more of my family's life has happened around it than anywhere else.

Part of the reason is practical. Our table stands a few steps from the stove and the fridge, so whoever is cooking can talk to whoever is sitting. When I was a boy, my father would peel potatoes at that table every evening while I did my homework across from him. He would peel, I would write, and between us we discussed everything from math to baseball.

A table also slows us down. It is hard to chew and hurry at the same time. When we sit down to eat, we have to stay for a while, to chew, to listen and to answer.

Every family has its specialty, and the table is where it is served. Our specialty is an apple cake, a recipe the family has always attributed to my great-grandmother. My mother admits, however, that she has changed almost everything in it, so perhaps it should be attributed to her. Each of my aunts makes her own variant, and every Thanksgiving, when the whole family squeezes around our table, the variants are tasted side by side and judged with great care. No variant has ever won. Thanksgiving at our house is less a meal than a long, happy argument about cake.

Of course, not every moment at the kitchen table is a happy one. It is also where bills are opened and bad news is shared. Some families, too, have little time to sit together; for them, dinner is something eaten standing at the open fridge. A table cannot, by itself, make a family close.

But perhaps this is exactly why the table matters. Because it hosts hard conversations as well as easy ones, it teaches us to have both. When I told my parents that I wanted to leave a steady job and train as a nurse, I told them at the kitchen table. They were worried, and they said so. But they were also supportive, and their supportive questions helped me more than any advice.

For my parents' anniversary last year, we threw a real bash, with music, a rented hall and a hundred guests. It was a wonderful bash. Yet what I remember best is the next morning, when the five of us sat around the old table, eating the last of the cake and laughing about the night before.

Questions:
What is the writer's family table like?
It is made of pine, one leg is slightly short, and its surface carries the marks of thirty years of family life.
What did the writer's father do at the table every evening?
He would peel potatoes while the writer did his homework.
Who is the family's specialty attributed to?
The apple cake is attributed to the writer's great-grandmother, although his mother has changed almost everything in it.
How were the writer's parents supportive when he wanted to train as a nurse?
They were worried, but they asked supportive questions that helped him more than any advice.
What does the writer remember best about the anniversary bash?
He remembers the next morning, when the family sat around the old table eating the last of the cake.

lessons.title: The Idea of Home
lessons.summary: Through a friend who grew up in many countries, the writer comes to see home as something people build together.
lessons.text:
What is home? For most of my life, I would have answered without thinking: a house, an address, a place on a map. I no longer find the question so simple.

My friend Ana grew up in more places than she can easily list. Her parents were missionary doctors, and the family moved every few years. They lived on a small isle in the Pacific, where the only shop sold rice, soap and fishing line, and later in two neighboring countries in East Africa. When people ask Ana where she is from, she usually pauses. "Do you mean where I was born," she says, "or where I feel at home?"

Many would say that home is simply the place where we were born and raised, and there is truth in this. The place of our childhood shapes us in ways we cannot fully see: the food we find comforting, the landscape that looks right to us, the accent we never quite lose. Sports fans often feel an almost tribal loyalty to the team of the town where they grew up, even decades after they have moved away. That tribal feeling is a way of saying: this is where I began.

Nonetheless, I do not think a place alone can be the whole answer. Ask Ana about the isle, and she will not describe the beaches. She will describe the family next door who taught her to swim, the woman who sold bread from her kitchen window, and the missionary nurse who read her stories at night. Her home was made of people more than places.

My own experience points the same way. When I moved to a new city after college, I packed everything I owned in boxes from a liquor store, because liquor stores always have strong boxes to give away. For weeks, my apartment felt like a hotel. What finally made it feel like home was not the furniture. It was the evening my neighbor knocked on the door with a plate of cookies, and the Saturday I helped the family in the neighboring apartment erect a small fence around the garden behind our building. We erected it badly, and it still leans to one side, but every time I walk past it, I feel that I belong.

If home were only the place of our birth, those of us who move would have lost it forever. But if home is something we build, out of habits, friendships and small favors, then we can build it again wherever we are. It takes time and effort. Nonetheless, it can be done.

Ana once told me that home is the place where someone would notice if you did not come back. I have not found a better definition.

Questions:
Why did Ana's family move every few years?
They moved because her parents were missionary doctors.
What kind of loyalty do many sports fans feel?
They feel an almost tribal loyalty to the team of the town where they grew up.
What does Ana describe when people ask her about the isle?
She describes the people: the family who taught her to swim, the woman who sold bread and the missionary nurse who read her stories.
Why did the writer pack his things in boxes from a liquor store?
Liquor stores always have strong boxes to give away.
What made the writer's new apartment feel like home?
His neighbor's visit with cookies and the day he helped the neighboring family erect a fence made it feel like home.

lessons.title: On Disagreeing Well
lessons.summary: Remembering his grandfather's dinner-table rules, the writer argues that disagreeing, done well, helps people understand each other.
lessons.text:
In my family, dinner always came with an argument. My grandfather believed that a meal without a debate was a meal wasted, and he raised his children to defend their opinions at the table. Some of my best memories come from those evenings. So, frankly, do some of my worst.

Disagreeing has a bad reputation these days, and it is easy to see why. Read the comments under almost any article online, and you will find people yelling at each other in capital letters. Every small story seems to cause outrage, and the outrage fades only when a new story arrives to replace it. When two opposing sides speak only to defeat each other, a conversation becomes a kind of warfare, with winners, losers and no peace in sight. It is disturbing to watch, and even more disturbing to take part in.

One might conclude that the wisest thing is to avoid arguments altogether: to change the subject, smile and keep the peace. Not every dinner needs to become a debate, and not every opinion needs to be shared.

Yet the opposite of warfare is not silence. It is disagreeing well, which is a skill that can be learned. My grandfather, for all his love of argument, had firm rules. Nobody was allowed to interrupt or to make it personal. If you made a claim about facts, you had to be ready to give a citation, even if the citation was only "I read it in the newspaper." He acted as a kind of referee, and when voices rose, the referee simply lifted his hand until there was quiet.

His most valuable rule was this: before you could oppose an idea, you had to explain it in your own words, so fairly that the person who held it would accept your summary. It is surprisingly hard to do. Once, our town planned to repeal a rule that kept cars out of the main square on weekends. My cousin wanted the town to repeal it, because her small coffee shop on the square was losing customers. I did not, because I loved the quiet square. Before I could oppose her, I had to describe her point of view, and in doing so I understood her worry for the first time. We still disagreed, but as two cousins, not as two opposing armies.

That, perhaps, is the real difference. Yelling aims to win. Disagreeing well aims to understand, even when understanding does not lead to agreement. Rarely did anyone change their mind at my grandfather's table. But we always left it knowing each other a little better, and I cannot imagine a better outcome for an argument.

Questions:
What did the writer's grandfather believe about meals?
He believed that a meal without a debate was a meal wasted.
What happens when two opposing sides speak only to defeat each other?
The conversation becomes a kind of warfare, with winners, losers and no peace in sight.
How did the grandfather act as a referee?
When voices rose, he lifted his hand until there was quiet.
What did you have to do before you could oppose an idea?
You had to explain it in your own words so fairly that the person who held it would accept your summary.
Why did the writer's cousin want the town to repeal the rule?
Her coffee shop on the square was losing customers.

lessons.title: The Saturday List
lessons.summary: Remembering his father's weekly trips around town, the writer weighs the ease of online shopping against the value of small errands.
lessons.text:
Every Saturday morning, my father sat down at the kitchen table with a pencil and wrote what he called "the list." It rarely changed: light bulbs, shampoo, something from the pharmacy, a stop at the hardware store and another at the bank. Then he drove his old pickup truck around town for three hours, crossing off each item as he went. As a teenager, I sometimes rode with him in the pickup, and I thought it was the most boring way a person could spend a morning.

Today, most of those trips are no longer necessary. I can order shampoo with a single click and have it at my door the next day. My medicine arrives by mail from a large pharmaceutical company I have never seen. For a parent with small children, or for someone who is ill or works long hours, this saves time that is badly needed, and I would not want to give it up.

And yet, in spite of all this convenience, I find myself missing the list.

At the hardware store, my father never had to explain what he needed. The man behind the counter knew that our kitchen lamp took a 60-watt bulb and the porch light a 40-watt one. When my father mentioned the black mold in our bathroom, the man walked him to the right shelf and told him how to keep the mold from coming back. At the pharmacy, the woman at the counter asked about my grandmother's knee before she handed over pills made in some distant pharmaceutical factory. And at the grocery store, my father would hold up a bottle of shampoo, read the price and announce, "This is highway robbery," an old way of saying that something costs far too much. He said it every week. Every week, in spite of the highway robbery, he paid.

My father, in other words, was a fixture of our town. A fixture is something fixed in place, like a light on a ceiling, and the word also describes a person who is always there. People expected to see him on Saturday, and when he was ill one winter, three store owners asked me where he was.

None of this can be ordered online. A website knows what I bought last time, but it does not know me.

So I have kept a small version of the list. Most things still arrive at my door. But on Saturday mornings, I walk to the hardware store and the pharmacy and buy one or two things I could easily have ordered. It costs me an hour. In return, I am slowly becoming a fixture myself.

Questions:
How did the writer's father travel around town on Saturday?
He drove his old pickup truck.
Why is online shopping a real help, according to the writer?
It saves time for parents with small children and for people who are ill or work long hours.
What did the man at the hardware store know?
He knew that the kitchen lamp took a 60-watt bulb and the porch light a 40-watt one.
What did the father mean when he said "This is highway robbery"?
He meant that the shampoo cost far too much.
Why does the writer call his father a fixture of the town?
People expected to see him every Saturday, and they asked about him when he was ill.

lessons.title: The Questions Children Ask
lessons.summary: The writer's young nephew asks a hundred questions a day, and the writer concludes that the best answer is often to find out together.
lessons.text:
My nephew is six, and on an ordinary day he asks about a hundred questions. Why is the sky blue? What happened to the dinosaurs? How small is an atom? If you cut an atom in half, what is left? He asks them in the car, in the bath and, most often, just before he goes to sleep.

Some of his questions are bizarre, at least to an adult. Last week, he wanted to know whether fish ever need a drink of water, and whether a dinosaur could have swum across the ocean. At first, such bizarre questions made me smile and change the subject. Lately, I have come to think that they deserve better.

There is, to be fair, another side to this. Answering a hundred questions a day is tiring, and no adult knows every answer. Some parents also feel that children should find things out for themselves, and that an adult who explains everything takes away the pleasure of discovery. Both points are fair. A child who receives a long lecture for every question will soon learn to stop asking.

Still, I believe that children's questions are where learning begins. Not long ago, I took my nephew to a natural history museum. He ran straight to the great dinosaur in the main hall, and then, to my surprise, spent half an hour in a quiet room full of insects in glass cases. Each specimen had a small card with its name and the place where it had been found. He read every card he could, asked me to read the rest, and wanted to know who had found each specimen and how.

In the next room, there was a short film about lions. A mother lion was teaching her cubs to hunt, and the cubs kept missing their prey, a group of small deer, because they could not keep still. My nephew laughed, and then he asked a question I could not answer: "Do the cubs feel bad when the prey gets away?" I told him honestly that I did not know. "Let's find out," I said, and that evening we read about lions together until he fell asleep.

I do not think my nephew is an exceptional child. Almost every child asks this many questions, and almost every child, around the age of ten or twelve, begins to ask fewer. What is exceptional is the adult who keeps asking long after school has ended. Perhaps the best gift we can give children is not the answers but the habit of looking for them, and the knowledge that "I don't know" is not the end of a conversation but the beginning of one.

Questions:
When does the writer's nephew ask most of his questions?
He asks them most often just before he goes to sleep.
What bizarre questions did the nephew ask last week?
He asked whether fish ever need a drink of water and whether a dinosaur could have swum across the ocean.
What was on the small card next to each specimen in the museum?
Each card had the specimen's name and the place where it had been found.
Why did the lion cubs keep missing their prey?
They kept missing their prey because they could not keep still.
What does the writer think is exceptional?
He thinks the adult who keeps asking questions long after school has ended is exceptional.
